title: Two kinds of moderate Democrats
gist: Yglesias distinguishes 'Tactical Moderates' from 'True Believer' moderates in the Democratic Party, using Abigail Spanberger, Joe Manchin, Susan Collins, and Ed Case as case studies, and argues that after a decade of factional warfare, moderates need a substantive conviction-based agenda (deficit reduction, permitting reform, school accountability) rather than just electability arguments to win the party's heart.

insights.claim: Democratic moderates split into two hard-to-distinguish types: 'Tactical Moderates' who moderate only because their district requires it, and 'True Believers' who hold moderate positions from genuine conviction; the distinction only becomes visible when a politician takes a position that runs against their own electoral self-interest.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Track moderate politicians for positions taken against their own electoral incentive as the real tell of conviction, rather than trusting campaign rhetoric about being a 'True Believer.'
insights.quote: It can be a little hard to tell the difference because if you’re moderate for tactical reasons, you’re of course going to say that you’re a True Believer.
insights.locator: opening paragraph, 'Yesterday, I wrote about the distinction'

insights.claim: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger's opposition to mandating collective bargaining for local government employees is read as evidence of genuine, not tactical, moderation, because Virginia's one-term gubernatorial limit and status as a federally safe-blue state give her no career incentive to buck the state's Progressive Establishment legislature.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Spanberger's willingness to clash with her own legislature on labor policy suggests she could become a genuine conviction-moderate national figure after her governorship, worth tracking for future federal ambitions.
insights.locator: 'Virginia only allows governors to serve one term'

insights.claim: Sarah McBride's appearance on 'The Ezra Klein Show' reflected an attempt at tactical retreat from the Democratic position favoring trans women's participation in competitive women's sports, while Martina Navratilova is instead arguing the party's current position is substantively wrong — illustrating the tactical-vs-conviction split playing out on a single live issue.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Watch for further elite Democratic repositioning on trans-athlete policy as an electorally costly issue moderates are quietly trying to exit.
insights.locator: 'When Sarah McBride went on “The Ezra Klein Show”'

insights.claim: Former Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards shows tactical moderation can still win in deep-red states — no candidate with progressive positions on guns or abortion could have won a Louisiana governorship — and Yglesias argues Democrats should recruit more Edwards-style tactical moderates in the Deep South specifically to open a path toward Medicaid expansion.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Red-state Medicaid expansion odds rise if Democrats prioritize recruiting Edwards-style tactical moderates for governor and Senate races over ideological purity — relevant for healthcare-sector watchers tracking the expansion-state count.
insights.locator: 'I do not agree with John Bel Edwards’s positions'

insights.claim: Yglesias argues tactical moderation has diminishing returns for Democrats going forward: expanding electoral reach via moderate recruiting in red states is still worthwhile, but actually capturing the 'heart' of the party requires arguments grounded in conviction on the merits, not just electability framing.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Intra-party dynamics through 2028 will hinge on whether moderates pivot from electability arguments to substantive policy fights — relevant for handicapping the 2028 Democratic primary field.
insights.locator: 'But I also think moderate Democrats are running on fumes'

insights.claim: Democrats' 2012 and 2018 West Virginia Senate wins with Joe Manchin were, in Yglesias's telling, largely a matter of luck — no conventional progressive Democrat could have won those races in that state.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Illustrates how thin the pre-2024 Democratic Senate majority math was and why losing the WV seat permanently reshaped the map.
insights.locator: 'Consider former Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia'

insights.claim: In 2021–22, progressives wanted Joe Manchin to abandon caution and vote to abolish the filibuster and pass a sweeping progressive agenda, reasoning he was already doomed for re-election in 2024 anyway (he ultimately did not run again) — the 'YOLO it' logic of tactical moderation taken to its endpoint.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows how progressive strategic calculus treats a moderate's vote as expendable once electoral survival looks hopeless — a pattern to watch with future 'doomed' moderate senators.
insights.locator: 'what they wanted him to do in 2021–22 was YOLO it'

insights.claim: Harry Reid's old joke that Susan Collins 'will always be with us except when we need her vote' captures Democratic frustration that Collins's bipartisan reputation rarely translates into decisive support at the moments that matter most.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Useful shorthand for evaluating any 'moderate' senator's real legislative value — track roll-call decisiveness, not press-friendly breaks with party.
insights.quote: she’ll always be with us except when we need her vote
insights.locator: 'Harry Reid had an old joke about Susan Collins'

insights.claim: Despite the Reid joke's cynicism, Susan Collins cast decisive votes in favor of the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, and against the 2017 Affordable Care Act repeal — showing her moderation has produced real, consequential outcomes at key moments, not just symbolic breaks with her party.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Collins remains a genuine swing vote worth pricing into any close Senate legislative forecast (healthcare, financial regulation) despite her low national profile.
insights.locator: 'Collins provided decisive votes in favor of'

insights.claim: Susan Collins has avoided a serious MAGA primary challenger, unlike Texas Senator John Cornyn, despite occasionally criticizing Trump, because she maintains a sufficiently cordial relationship with the Trump White House and has never meaningfully collaborated with Democrats to restrain him.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Collins's survival model (symbolic dissent plus substantive deference) is a template other Republican moderates may copy to avoid primary threats — relevant to 2026/2028 GOP Senate primary risk.
insights.locator: 'she never faced a serious MAGA challenger'

insights.claim: Yglesias's broader framework: there is probably no such thing as a politician who privately agrees entirely with their party base but is simply skilled at faking moderation to win repeatedly in tough states — representing a divergent constituency over time tends to genuinely change a politician's views by exposing real flaws in their own coalition's demands.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Analysts modeling 'moderate' politicians as pure performers should expect some of their deviations to persist even after electoral pressure eases.
insights.locator: 'There’s probably just no such thing as a politician'

insights.claim: Yglesias states he personally agrees with Manchin that the Build Back Better legislation pushed by congressional Democratic leadership was inflationary, and that Manchin's push toward permitting reform and innovation-focused clean energy policy (rather than pipeline-blocking) was correct on the merits, though he disagrees with Manchin's defense of the filibuster; he adds the U.S. would be better off today had Democrats more fully embraced Manchin's permitting legislation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals continued elite-Democratic-commentariat appetite for bipartisan permitting reform as a more durable path to clean-energy buildout than spending-led approaches — relevant to future energy permitting legislation odds.
insights.locator: 'Manchin was wrong on the merits about some important stuff'

themes.theme: True Believers and the Ed Case model

insights.claim: Hawaii Representative Ed Case has overperformed the Split Ticket database's generic partisan baseline by 17 points (2018), 14 points (2020), 18 points (2022), and 17 points (2024), despite representing a district Kamala Harris won 62-37 — meaning there is no electability rationale for his moderate positioning; he is moderate purely from conviction.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Case is a rare empirical case for isolating 'true believer' moderation from tactical moderation — a useful benchmark when assessing whether a politician's centrism is genuine.
insights.locator: 'In the Split Ticket database, he overperformed'

insights.claim: Ed Case survived a 2026 primary challenge attacking his support for the SAVE America Act purely by arguing on the merits, with no electability case to make, after previously losing statewide primaries for governor and twice for Senate to more progressive Hawaii Democratic electorates.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a durable base of conviction-moderate primary voters can exist even in deep-blue electorates — worth tracking for other conviction moderates facing 2026–28 primaries.
insights.locator: 'He faced a primary challenge this cycle'

insights.claim: Elizabeth Warren is, per the same overperformance framework, 'an absolutely terrible electoral underperformer,' but it doesn't matter politically because Massachusetts is a safe Democratic state where Harris did even slightly worse statewide than she did in Case's Hawaii district.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Individual candidate overperformance metrics are only politically consequential in competitive seats — a reminder not to over-read such stats for safe-seat incumbents.
insights.locator: 'Elizabeth Warren is, as Slow Boring readers know'

insights.claim: Yglesias coins 'dog-whistle moderation' (or 'meta-moderation') for members who speak abstractly about meeting voters where they are without taking concrete unpopular positions, and argues this framing is wrong on the causal facts: Iowa's shift from an Obama-Obama state to a Trump-Trump-Trump state was driven by mainstream Democrats moving left, not by Bernie Sanders or the insurgent left, who were present in the party the whole time.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts a common moderate talking point blaming 'the groups'/insurgent left for red-state losses — a useful check when reading future moderate commentary on electoral setbacks.
insights.quote: Iowa didn’t flip from being an Obama-Obama state to a Trump-Trump-Trump state because of Bernie Sanders
insights.locator: 'These types tend to complain a lot about the Insurgent Left'

themes.theme: Defining the actual moderate policy agenda

insights.claim: Responding to Axios's Mike Zapler ('The Democratic Establishment's Ideas Deficit'), Yglesias argues congressional Democratic leadership under Biden-Harris (Schumer/Jeffries) never actually pursued a centrist agenda — their program (raising the tax share of GDP with a more progressive code, funneling new revenue into clean energy and social spending, abortion rights, affirmative action, neo-Brandeisian antitrust) is simply a subset of the progressive agenda, tempered by electoral prudence and court losses, not a distinct centrist program.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'moderate establishment has no ideas' narrative — useful for handicapping whether a genuinely distinct centrist Democratic platform emerges before 2028.
insights.locator: 'Mike Zapler wrote a piece for Axios this week'

insights.claim: Domestic U.S. oil-and-gas production reached record levels under the Biden-Harris administration, but only after the administration's own efforts to halt new leases were blocked in court — evidence, per Yglesias, that the administration's actual policy preference was restrictive even though the realized outcome looked production-friendly.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Energy analysts should attribute recent record U.S. oil/gas output to court-forced continuity of leasing rather than deliberate administration policy — relevant to modeling future administrations' leasing posture.
insights.quote: domestic oil-and-gas production reached new record levels but only after efforts to halt new leases were blocked in court
insights.locator: 'On their watch, domestic oil-and-gas production'

insights.claim: Yglesias lays out a concrete alternative centrist Democratic agenda: deficit reduction to ease inflation and interest rates; 'clean energy abundance' paired with championing domestic fossil-fuel production over imports; performance pay for teachers; supply-side deregulation of housing and healthcare; and treating crime control and border security as legitimate core state functions rather than reluctant concessions.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete policy checklist for evaluating whether any 2028 Democratic candidate is a genuine conviction-centrist versus a rhetorical moderate.
insights.locator: 'It would emphasize deficit reduction to put downward pressure'

insights.claim: Yglesias cites New York and California public schools performing worse at teaching kids to read than Mississippi's as an embarrassing example of blue-state governance failing to convert resource advantages into outcomes.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for evaluating blue-state education policy credibility — worth tracking state reading-proficiency data (e.g., NAEP) as a scorecard.
insights.quote: It’s really shameful for New York and California to be worse at teaching kids to read than Mississippi
insights.locator: 'It’s really shameful for New York and California'

insights.claim: Yglesias suggests a 2028 Democratic presidential campaign could provide the political cover needed to overcome the collective-action problem currently preventing individual moderate Democrats from directly 'taking on the groups' (progressive advocacy infrastructure).
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Watch the 2028 Democratic primary field for a candidate explicitly running against progressive advocacy groups as a structural, not just personal, strategy.
insights.locator: 'The collective action problem around taking on the groups'
